title: WOE IS ME.
paragraphs: WOE IS ME.
That was not a sermon.
That was a collapse.
A prophet—chosen, trained, anointed—suddenly realizes he cannot even stand in the presence of God.

Not because he saw demons.
Not because he saw judgment.
But because he saw holiness.
In Isaiah 6, the prophet steps into the temple and something happens that shatters him forever.
He sees the Lord.

High.
Lifted up.
The train of His robe filling the temple.
Seraphim hover in blazing fire above the throne, covering their faces, crying to one another:

“Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts;
the whole earth is full of His glory!” (Isaiah 6:3)
The doorposts shake.
The room fills with smoke.
And suddenly Isaiah realizes something terrifying.
He does not belong there.
Not because he is worse than others.
But because God is holier than he ever imagined.
So the prophet does not say:
“Lord, look at their sin.”
He says something far more honest.
“Woe is me! For I am undone.” (Isaiah 6:5)
Undone.
The Hebrew idea is devastating.
It means ruined… destroyed… falling apart inside.
Why?

“Because I am a man of unclean lips,
and I dwell among a people of unclean lips.”
The mouth that preached for God suddenly feels polluted.
The lips that spoke prophecy now feel unworthy to whisper His name.
Isaiah had likely spent years confronting Israel’s sin.
But now the light is turned inward.
And when the holiness of God shines on a human soul, something happens that religion cannot fake.
Masks fall.
Pretending dies.
Comparison evaporates.
Because standing before God is not like standing before other people.
Among people, we can look righteous.
Among people, we can hide.
Among people, we can curate our image.
But before the blazing purity of God—
everything is exposed.
Your pride.
Your secret habits.
Your hidden bitterness.
Your private compromises.
The things nobody else sees.
Suddenly Isaiah realizes:
Even a prophet is unclean.
And this is where many people misunderstand the Bible.
They think God exposes sin because He wants to shame people.
But watch what happens next.
God does not destroy Isaiah.
He cleanses him.
A seraph flies from the altar holding a burning coal.
Fire from the place of sacrifice.
The angel touches Isaiah’s lips and declares:
Do you see the pattern?
God reveals.
Then God redeems.
Conviction is not the end of the story.
It is the doorway to grace.
That burning coal from the altar was a shadow.
A preview.
A symbol pointing forward.
Because one day, the ultimate sacrifice would come.
Not a coal.
Not an animal offering.
But Jesus Christ Himself.
The cross is where holiness and mercy collide.
Where God does not ignore sin—but pays for it.
Where the guilt that crushes us is carried by the Son of God.
Where the unclean are washed clean.
Isaiah received a coal.
We receive a crucified Savior.
And when grace touches a life, everything changes.
The same man who cried “Woe is me” suddenly hears a question echo through heaven.

“Whom shall I send?
And who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8)
And Isaiah answers with one of the most courageous responses in Scripture.
“Here am I. Send me.”
Do you see the transformation?

Before grace:
Woe is me.

After grace:
Send me.
God does not call perfect people.
He calls forgiven people.
The greatest danger in the church today is not weakness.
It is pretending we are strong.
Pretending we are clean.
Pretending we do not need grace.
But heaven moves when a person finally says what Isaiah said.
Not:
“Look at everyone else.”
But:
“Lord… it’s me.”
And the miracle of the Gospel is this:
Jesus does not run from ruined people.
He restores them.
The lips that once spoke lies become lips that speak life.
The heart that once carried shame becomes a vessel of grace.
The sinner becomes a messenger.
And the story that shame tried to bury becomes the testimony God uses to heal others.
Maybe you know the feeling Isaiah felt.
The moment when your soul whispers:
“I am not worthy.”
You are right.
None of us are.
But that is exactly why Jesus came.
Not for the polished.
Not for the perfect.
Not for the religious elite.
He came for the ruined.
For the broken.
For the ones who know deep down they cannot cleanse themselves.
And when His grace touches your life, your story does not end with “Woe is me.”
It begins again with:
“Here am I. Send me.”

Because the same God who exposes your sin
also removes your guilt
and gives your life a mission.
Sit with it.
Ask God the same question Isaiah faced.
“Lord… what in me needs cleansing?”
And if you already know Jesus, remember this:
Your past does not disqualify you.
Grace rewrites everything.
Because heaven is still asking the question.
And someone reading this might be the next Isaiah.
“We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.”
